author.name: William Shakespeare
author.biography: Shakespeare left Stratford-upon-Avon for a career in London's theatres, where he worked as an actor, playwright and company shareholder. He knew stories as things people performed before other people, with attention, sympathy and judgment changing from moment to moment. Shakespeare drew on Roman history to examine the tension between public reputation and private attachment. His theatrical Cleopatra also exposes how power can depend on controlling the story told about oneself.

hook.text: Would you give up being important to stay with the person you love?

paragraphs: Antony has responsibilities across the Roman world and a life with Cleopatra in Egypt that makes those responsibilities feel distant. Other people are watching the distance grow and calculating what it might offer them.

Shakespeare refuses to make either world sufficient. Political discipline can look cold and calculating; passionate freedom can become careless of the people required to sustain it. Antony and Cleopatra are lovers and rulers, so their private choices travel far beyond the room in which they are made.

Their language can make life seem larger, more generous and more beautiful. It can also make self-deception magnificent. The play asks what happens when a person's public identity and deepest attachment demand incompatible performances.
Listen for the struggle to determine how an action will be remembered. Which would matter more to you: living the life you wanted, or being seen to have lived a great one?

orientation.text: The action moves between Roman and Egyptian political worlds. Antony, Cleopatra and Octavius Caesar each have a different understanding of what power requires.
